Question: How do you compare and contrast the way that theory is used among lay people and scientists? How does or doesn’t evolution fit for the definition of a scientific theory?
Answer: First of all, let’s look as how the term “theory” is used by lay people: a “theory” is just an idea i have about something, an hypothesis at best. That is not what a scientific theory is. Scientists observe facts, and then theorize about how those facts happen and why. They then formulate an hypothesis (the lay person would call it a “theory”), which must include predictions (if this, then that), then conduct experiments in order to find out if their hypothesis correctly applies to the facts observed. If the experiments agree with their hypothesis, and the experiments agree with the predictions, then we have a theory. A theory, thus, is an explanation of observed facts, and establish a theoretical construct that describes how the facts happen and why. So, a theory is published by the scientist, to be further peer reviewed, his experiments reproduced by others, and if no single experiment contradicts it and it is considered accurate by the scientific community, then it is established. From then on, it becomes a tool for those that study that specific issue, and allows them to further their knowledge on the issue. So, a scientific theory is the highest level of certainty that science can produce. It is the best possible description of how and why what we observe happens. As to the theory of evolution, it is a scientific theory. Enough said. The fact that species evolve over time was already known and accepted for centuries, but it took Darwin to for the first time provide an accurate description of the hows and whys.

Higher power mods use two or even three batteries to be able to work safely with a 100 W or higher load. Don’t mess with used batteries. Those old ICR batteries were the responsible for most of the accidents involving batteries that happened with vaping in the past, because they are way less tolerant to an overcharge and can fail almost immediately. Question: Why do the British revere Field Marshal Montgomery even though he was a fairly incompetent strategist and tactician (his failed Operation Market Garden plan, as well as only winning battles when he had superior manpower)?
Answer: Montgomery and the Americans had a different military culture. The American doctrine was to always attack, to always maintain the front active, to be always proactive. Montgomery had a different doctrine. He had already two years of experience under his belt, and he knew the German tactics well. I guess the critical point where the two cultures clashed was the Battle of the Bulge. The German attack cut the American forces in half, and Eisenhower gave the command of all the forces in the north of the bulge to Montgomery, while Bradley would command the forces in the south. The Americans, faithful to their doctrine, poured reinforcements into Bastogne in order to prevent it from falling, to take the fight to the Germans at all costs. And they did it brilliantly. However, that was not the idea that Montgomery had of the battle. He knew that the push would force the Germans to overextend, and consolidated the front to prepare a general counter-attack for when the Germans would be the most vulnerable. He would prefer the Americans to evacuate Bastogne and prepare to attack at the right time. So, while the Americans were fighting in Bastogne, Montgomery, sticking to his plan, did nothing, while reorganizing the front and prepare it to attack. Not that anything that he could do at that time would in any way help the Americans in the south. It was a clash of different war cultures, and Montgomery’s inaction infuriated the Americans in the south, and made them even doubt his will to fight. Eventually, the Germans overextended, as was inevitable, and, helped by the presence of the Americans in Bastogne, Montgomery unleashed a masterfully executed counter-attack that completely destroyed the Germans, forcing them to retreat all the way back to Germany, leaving almost all of their tanks and other materials behind. And he managed to do it while keeping the casualties low, which was his foremost concern. As to Operation Market Garden, the Germans had already experienced the Invasion of Crete by paratroopers, which backfired horribly, to the point of them giving up on any further paratrooper attack in the future. The Allies still hadn’t have that experience, which is in part why the operation failed. It is always easy to criticize looking back, but in war, the fog of war is always present.

Question: What happens when a change is committed to Linux? How long does it take before I can update my machine with that code?
Answer: Depends on the “owners” of the distribution you are using. I will give the example of Debian (from which many distributions derive, including Ubuntu). Debian has 3 sets of repositories: stable (the current Debian distribution) testing (the one that will be the nest stable distribution) and unstable (where every new software is stored). Software belonging to the OS will enter the unstable repository, then migrate to testing after being checked and in time become the next stable distribution. The software will continue to receive updates until the testing repository is “frozen”, which means that the current selection of software will not be changed until the new stable distribution is ready for release. Critical updates, however, will continue to be added. Each cycle will take around 2 years, although Debian has the policy of “release when ready” and doesn’t depend on any preset calendar. That insures that Debian distributions are very stable and secure, but a bit outdated regarding the latest improvements. Which is why Ubuntu is based on a snapshot of Debian testing, and then prepared and tested for each Ubuntu release. Which means that Ubuntu is more up to date than Debian, although it might not be as stable. However, there are distributions built on top of Debian unstable, having the state of the art software, although yet unproven. So, the user can chose the level of innovation versus stability. Regarding the common apps everyone uses, like Firefox or LibreOffice, or VLC, usually the last updates reach the distributions repositories and become available very quickly, since they are not system critical. Regardless of all that, when a vulnerability is found, a patch is made overnight and an update will be released, frequently in the next day.

Question: What are some unique aspects of Ravel’s compositions?
Answer: Ravel studied chords and sonority. Try a simple test: . Get a piano . Play a simple major chord, like Do-mi-so-do. . Now, press the pedal and play it again without releasing the pedal . Listen The sound is very different. The reason is that, when all the piano cords are released, they all vibrate. Some more than others, depending on the notes played. It is that effect that gives a “spacial” feel to the chord you play. Ravel studied that. Although the Braun tube had not been invented yet, he could identify many of those extra notes that would make that “spacial” effect of pressing the piano pedal. And so, he augmented the chords, including extra notes. This technique gave his music a specific sonority, which is part of the reason why many consider him the best orchestrator of all time. Worth mentioning Messiaen, who, using the Braun tube to look at sound, further extended the chords, going much further than Ravel.

Question: Modern History of World: What are some cool/unusual facts about soldiers in WWI and WWII?
Answer: Meet Anibal Milhais, a Portuguese foot soldier. He was part of the Portuguese Expeditionary Force in Flanders during WW I. At the start of 1918, Germany mounted its last ditch offensive in the western front (Russia had already withdrawn from the war). The offensive, in Flanders, was meant to open a breach in the very weakened First British Army, which included 2 divisions of the Portuguese Expeditionary Force. The attack was overwhelming, and after suffering heavy losses both the British and Portuguese retreated. Milhais remained alone with his Lewis machine gun. And, for three days, he stopped the assault of two German regiments, giving enough time for the British and Portuguese to retreat, playing a cat and mouse game, cautiously choosing his position and often moving to another position if he thought he had been spotted. The Germans decided to go around his position, which was good, because he had run out of ammunition. He later found himself, completely alone, behind enemy lines, having spent all his ammunition. From Wikipedia: “On the third day, Milhais, still carrying his Lewis gun, rescued a Scottish major from a swamp, and the two reached Allied lines.” “A few months later, Milhais once again held back a German assault single-handed with his Lewis gun, allowing a Belgian unit to retreat safely to a secondary trench without casualties. Both the British observers present in the scene and the Belgian commander included his action in their reports.” “Milhais was awarded the highest Portuguese distinction - the Order of the Tower and Sword - and the French Légion d’Honneur, delivered on the battlefield before 15,000 Allied soldiers.” “On July 15, 1918, the Order of Service of the Battalion published a commendation, given by Major Ferreira do Amaral, which described his action as having been worth a million men, hence the nickname by which he became known: "Soldier Millions".” Aníbal Milhais - Wikipedia Battle of the Lys (1918) - Wikipedia
